newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH ZLOTY SEEN BULLISH ON FUNDAMENTALS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH ZLOTY SEEN BULLISH ON FUNDAMENTALS.

text.p: The Polish zloty, quietly firming against the basket of currencies over the last few weeks, was stopped in its tracks by central bank interventions on Monday, but analysts say it would not give up its upward thrust easily.
The National Bank of Poland has long tolerated the firming of the zloty without any reaction, but finally decided to cap it on Monday at four percent from the trading band centre.

Analysts estimated the National Bank of Poland's dollar- and mark-buying interventions on Monday drained some $80 million from the market pushing the Polish unit one percentage point lower to three percent from the band centre.

Analysts said the zloty's recent bull run was fuelled by start-of-year position taking in zloty instruments by foreign investors drawn by Poland's better then expected 1996 inflation and its plans to meet European Monetary Union criteria in 2004.

"People have got new amounts of money to invest in emerging markets and...they can't keep it in dollars, so at the beginning of the year you often get a rally," said Andrew Kenningham, economist at Merrill Lynch in London.
"I think the zloty is likely to stay bullish," he said.

Analysts also noted high real interest rates and the central bank's commitment to keeping them high to curb credit growth as well as the NBP's plans to reduce the zloty's monthly devaluation factor this year.
Dealers said the fundamental nature of the zloty's recent gains was likely to keep the Polish unit bullish in the near-term despite the threat of an NBP intervention.

"(Polish paper) is attractive because real interest rates are still high, the c.bank seems committed to keep them high, and because the crawling peg will be cut further in 1997," said Krassimir Katev, dealer at Paribas Capital Markets in London.

The zloty is now devalued one percent a month against a basket of currencies, in a mechanism known as the crawling peg, but the NBP has announced it planned zloty devaluation in 1997 at nine percent, which would entail a cut from current levels.

Analysts also noted the large scale of expected foreign direct and portfolio investment, which some put as high as $5 billion this year, as a factor which could largely offset the widening trade gap, seen around $8 billion in 1996.
Dealers said that with yields above 20 percent and inflation this year expected at 15-16 percent Polish 12 month or two-year fixed interest paper was very attractive.
"All this seems like a good reason to invest, since you get something like 8.5-9.5 percent rate of return in dollar terms," said a dealer at a London-based bank.

Dealers expected the central bank's Monday interventions would not deter foreign buyers as many saw the zloty's fall to three percent from the trading band centre from four percent this morning as an opportunity to buy it before it firms again.

"T-bill yields could still rise and attract foreign investors. And the zloty is likely to be under upward pressure as those who missed out when it was at four percent the first time want to be there the next time around," a dealer at a major investment bank in London said.
The Monday NBP interventions were the first since May 1996, when they usually came to stop the Polish unit at about 2.5-3.0 percent from the parity rate.
